key_terms.meaning: A chain of five blocks: transmitter, fiber, splices and connectors, any repeater or amplifier, and receiver; only two terminals talk.
The fraction of received bits that are wrong; a good digital link keeps BER at 10⁻⁹ or lower.
Ratio of received carrier power to noise power in the signal band, in dB; the quality measure for an analog link.
The smallest number of photons per bit (about 10 to 20) that a receiver needs when all other noise is removed.
Sum of every loss between source and detector, plus a margin, compared with the power the source gives and the receiver needs.
Extra decibels kept aside (usually 4 to 6 dB) for ageing of the source, connector wear and repair splices.
The minimum average optical power at the detector, in dBm, for the specified BER or CNR.
Loss per joint: about 0.05 to 0.1 dB for a fusion splice, 0.3 to 1 dB for a connector pair.
Check that the combined rise times of source, fiber and detector fit inside the bit period, t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.7 T for NRZ.
Pulse spreading in a multimode fiber because modes travel different path lengths; measured in ns/km.
Pulse spreading because different wavelengths travel at different speeds; coefficient D in ps/(nm·km).
The longest span the power budget allows: L<sub>att</sub> = (P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> − margin − joint losses) ÷ α.
The longest span the rise-time budget allows; found from the allowed fiber rise time and the fiber's dispersion.
Measure output power with a long length, cut back to a short length near the source, and take the difference in dB over the removed length.
Send a short pulse into a long fiber and measure how much it broadens; broadening ÷ length gives dispersion.
Modulate the source sinusoidally and measure how much the received sine wave shifts in phase as the wavelength is stepped.
NA = sin θ<sub>a</sub> = √(n₁² − n₂²), where θ<sub>a</sub> is the largest half-angle that is guided, and n₁, n₂ are core and cladding refractive indices.
The wavelength below which a single-mode fiber starts to carry the second mode; measured by bending or by scanning the transmitted power.
Width of the light spot leaving a single-mode fiber; measured from the far-field pattern, and it sets splice loss and bend loss.
ORL in dB = −10 log₁₀(P<sub>reflected</sub>/P<sub>incident</sub>); good connectors give better than 40 dB.

takeaways: A point-to-point link is designed block by block; every dB lost between source and detector must be paid for by source power or receiver sensitivity.
Digital links are judged by bit error rate, analog links by carrier-to-noise ratio, so the same fiber gives different answers for the two.
The power budget answers how far the signal reaches, the rise-time budget answers how fast it can go, and the link must pass both.
The shorter of the attenuation-limited and dispersion-limited lengths is the real maximum span.
Attenuation is a difference of two power readings, so the cutback method removes connector and launch uncertainties.
Dispersion is measured either by pulse broadening in time or by phase shift in frequency; both need a long fiber and a narrow source.
NA, cutoff wavelength and MFD are all read from the light that leaves the fiber, so they describe the fiber as the network sees it.
Field tests use the same ideas as lab tests, but with an OTDR, an optical power meter and a stable source that fit in a van.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on the two budgets — a full power budget table and a rise-time check for one numerical link — plus descriptions of the standard measurement set-ups with their precautions.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a digital point-to-point optical link and explain the job of each block. Why is BER used as the quality measure for a digital link and CNR for an analog link?
outline: Transmitter: drive circuit plus source, either LED or laser diode
Fiber cable with splices and connectors; repeaters or amplifiers on long routes
Receiver: photodiode, preamplifier, decision circuit
BER counts wrong bits after decision; the decision threshold and noise set it
Analog link carries a continuously varying signal, so the noise relative to the carrier, not the bit error, decides quality
Typical targets: BER 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻¹², CNR 50 dB or better for video

bank.q: Define link power budget. List every term that goes into it and state typical values for each.
outline: Budget: P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> = αL + α<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + α<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + margin
P<sub>T</sub> launched power in dBm, P<sub>R</sub> receiver sensitivity in dBm
Fiber loss 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm, 2 to 4 dB/km for plastic or POF
Connector pair 0.3 to 1 dB, fusion splice 0.05 to 0.1 dB
System margin 4 to 6 dB
Answer must say whether the budget passes and if not, what to change

bank.q: Explain the rise-time budget. State the rule for combining independent rise times and give the allowed system rise time for NRZ and RZ formats.
outline: Total rise time t<sub>sys</sub> = √(t<sub>tx</sub>² + t<sub>fiber</sub>² + t<sub>rx</sub>²)
t<sub>fiber</sub> from modal dispersion in multimode and from chromatic dispersion in single mode
NRZ: t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.7 T; RZ: t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.35 T, where T is one bit period
Why the square root: independent Gaussian broadening adds in variance
If the sum exceeds the limit, reduce length, narrow the source spectrum or lower the bit rate

bank.q: Describe the cutback method for measuring fiber attenuation, with a neat set-up, the formula used, and the precautions that make the result trustworthy.
outline: Launch a stable source into a long length L; record P₁ at the far end with a large-area detector
Cut the fiber back to a short length (about 2 m), keeping the launch condition identical, and record P₂
α = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁) ÷ (L₁ − L₂) in dB per unit length
Precautions: same launch, cladding-mode stripper, stable source, steady temperature, no change in detector position
Cutback kills launch and connector uncertainty because they appear in both readings

bank.q: A 1300 nm link has launched power −10 dBm, fiber loss 0.35 dB/km, length 40 km, two connector pairs at 0.8 dB each, four fusion splices at 0.1 dB each, receiver sensitivity −30 dBm and a system margin of 6 dB. Check the power budget and find the longest span that passes.
outline: Available power difference = −10 − (−30) = 20 dB
Fiber loss = 0.35 × 40 = 14 dB
Connectors = 1.6 dB, splices = 0.4 dB, margin = 6 dB
Total needed = 22 dB, which is more than 20 dB, so the link fails
Allowable fiber loss = 20 − 6 − 1.6 − 0.4 = 12 dB
Maximum length = 12 ÷ 0.35 = 34.3 km
Comment: shorten the span, reduce joints, use a more sensitive receiver, or add margin only after the check

bank.q: Rise times are 0.6 ns (source), 0.8 ns (modal), 1.2 ns (chromatic) and 0.5 ns (detector). Find the system rise time and test it against a 500 Mb/s NRZ link. What is the highest NRZ bit rate this link can carry?
outline: t<sub>sys</sub> = √(0.6² + 0.8² + 1.2² + 0.5²) ns
At 500 Mb/s NRZ, T = 2 ns and the limit is 0.7T = 1.4 ns
1.64 ns > 1.4 ns, so the link fails at 500 Mb/s
Largest allowed T = 1.64 ÷ 0.7 = 2.34 ns, so the highest bit rate is about 1 ÷ 2.34 ns ≈ 427 Mb/s
State clearly that dispersion, not loss, is the binding limit here

bank.q: A single-mode link must work at 2.5 Gb/s over one span. Fiber loss is 0.25 dB/km, dispersion coefficient 17 ps/(nm·km), source spectral width 0.1 nm, and the allowed fiber rise time is 40 ps. Check both limits for 80 km and say which one binds.
outline: Bit period T = 400 ps, NRZ limit t<sub>sys</sub> = 0.7T = 280 ps
Chromatic broadening = D × Δλ × L = 17 × 0.1 × 80 = 136 ps
Convert broadening to a rise time (the 0.44 factor for a Gaussian pulse) and square-add with the other rise times
Compare with 280 ps; also compute fiber loss = 0.25 × 80 = 20 dB and check against the power budget
Name the limit that gives the smaller allowable length
Suggest a remedy: narrower linewidth source, dispersion-shifted fiber or dispersion compensation

bank.q: A far-field scan of a step-index fiber shows the guided cone ending at a half-angle of 12°. The core index is 1.48. Find the numerical aperture, the cladding index and the maximum acceptance angle in air.
outline: NA = sin θ<sub>a</sub> = sin 12° ≈ 0.208
Use NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) to get n₂ = √(1.48² − 0.208²) ≈ 1.465
Index difference Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁ ≈ 0.010, so about 1 percent
State the measurement precaution: strip cladding modes and use the 5 percent intensity point rather than the visible edge
Mention that NA sets coupling loss from a source and bend sensitivity

bank.q: Prepare the power budget for a three-channel WDM link: a 1×4 splitter (7 dB), an add-drop multiplexer (2 dB), a demultiplexer (3 dB) and 25 km of fiber at 0.25 dB/km. If 30 dB of power difference is available, what margin is left?
outline: Fiber loss = 0.25 × 25 = 6.25 dB
Total passive loss = 7 + 2 + 3 = 12 dB
Sum = 18.25 dB
Margin left = 30 − 18.25 = 11.75 dB
Comment that WDM adds passives, not fiber, so the budget shrinks quickly
Note that splitters also reduce the per-channel power, so per-channel launch matters

bank.q: Compare time-domain and frequency-domain (phase-shift) measurement of dispersion. Which is preferred for a long single-mode link and why?
outline: Time domain: short pulse in, broadened pulse out, width difference divided by length gives dispersion
Frequency domain: sinusoidal modulation, measure phase as wavelength is stepped, then differentiate phase with wavelength
Time domain needs picosecond pulses and a fast detector, so it is simple but limited in resolution
Phase-shift gives higher resolution and works with narrow linewidth sources; slower because it scans wavelength
For long single-mode links with small dispersion, phase-shift is preferred
Both need a long fiber and careful referencing to remove the source and detector response

bank.q: You must design a 2.5 Gb/s link over 80 km of standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm. Using the power budget and the rise-time budget, decide whether the link works and identify the binding limit.
outline: Table of terms: launched power, sensitivity, fiber loss, joints, margin
Compute attenuation-limited length and compare with 80 km
Compute chromatic broadening from D and source linewidth, then the fiber rise time
Compare t<sub>sys</sub> with 0.7T = 280 ps
Conclude which limit gives the smaller span
Remedies: dispersion-compensating fiber, narrower laser, amplifier or regeneration

bank.q: Explain how an OTDR is used in the field for splice loss, fault location and return loss. Why do field readings differ from lab measurements?
outline: OTDR sends a pulse and plots backscattered power against distance
Slope of the trace gives attenuation; a step down is a splice or connector
Reflective spike at a connector gives reflectance; ORL from the total reflected power
Two-point and four-point methods for splice loss; the dead zone after a reflection
Differences: launch conditions, temperature, bending in trays, one-directional readings
Field checks also use power meter and stable source for end-to-end loss

bank.q: Why do cutoff wavelength and mode-field diameter matter in single-mode link design? Describe how each is measured.
outline: Below cutoff the fiber carries two modes and the link becomes noisy and unstable
Cutoff measured by transmitted-power scan over wavelength, or by the bend technique on a short loop
MFD sets splice loss and bend loss; matched MFD gives low loss
MFD measured from the far-field pattern and transformed to the near field
System rule: keep operation well above cutoff, and match MFDs at joints
Tolerance on MFD is tight in the cable specification

bank.q: Explain the carrier-to-noise ratio of an analog optical link. List the noise sources and show how the modulation index affects CNR.
outline: CNR = 10 log₁₀(½m²I²R ÷ noise power), with m the modulation index and I the average photocurrent
Noise sources: shot noise, thermal noise of the preamplifier, relative intensity noise of the laser
RIN dominates at high received power; thermal noise dominates at low power
Increasing m raises CNR but pushes the laser towards clipping
Typical CNR for video 50 dB or better
Analog links are used in CATV and radio-over-fiber

glossary.def: Loss of optical power along the fiber, quoted in dB per kilometre at a stated wavelength.
The time occupied by one bit; T = 1 ÷ bit rate, measured in seconds.
Light travelling in the cladding rather than the core; it must be stripped before a measurement or the reading is too high.
A removable joint between two fibers or a fiber and a device, typically losing 0.3 to 1 dB.
The wavelength below which a single-mode fiber begins to carry a second mode.
The length after a strong reflection in an OTDR trace where a second event cannot be seen.
Pulse spread per unit length per unit source linewidth, in ps/(nm·km).
The spread of light intensity measured far from the fiber end face; it gives NA and MFD.
A permanent joint made by melting two fiber ends together, typically losing 0.05 to 0.1 dB.
Fractional step between core and cladding index, Δ = (n₁ − n₂) ÷ n₁.
How light enters the fiber — spot size, angle and mode filling — which changes measured loss and NA.
Width of the optical power distribution in a single-mode fiber, close to but not equal to the core diameter.
The sine of the largest half-angle of a cone that the fiber guides; NA = √(n₁² − n₂²).
Ratio of reflected to incident power at a joint, expressed as a positive dB number.
Optical time-domain reflectometer; it sends pulses and reads backscatter to give loss, events and distance.
Extra decibels of power needed to hold the same BER when a new impairment such as dispersion is added.
The fraction of incident power reflected at a joint or end face; ORL in dB is its negative logarithm times ten.
Laser power fluctuation quoted in dB per hertz; it limits CNR at high received power.
Time for a pulse to swing from 10 percent to 90 percent of its final value.
Range of wavelengths emitted by the source; it multiplies with dispersion to spread the pulse.
Decibels reserved in the power budget for ageing, repairs and temperature, usually 4 to 6 dB.
Sending several wavelengths on one fiber; it adds multiplexers and demultiplexers to the power budget.
